comment: Daily-refreshed feed of clinical breakthroughs, regulatory events, and guideline shifts. `audience` is 'general' (everyday-actionable, plain-English) or 'technical' (specialist-only). Public surfaces filter to general by default.

items.headline: First OTC glucose monitor approved for children with diabetes
items.summary: The FDA approved the first over-the-counter continuous glucose monitor for children. This device allows blood sugar monitoring without a prescription.
items.why_it_matters: Parents can now buy a glucose monitor for their child without a prescription, making diabetes management easier at home.

items.headline: AI-Powered Eye Scan Improves Diabetes Vision Screening Accuracy
items.summary: An AI-enhanced eye scan system improved detection of diabetic eye disease in a clinical trial. It showed better diagnostic accuracy and reduced unnecessary referrals compared to standard screening.
items.why_it_matters: If you have diabetes, ask your doctor about AI-enhanced eye screenings for early detection of vision-threatening complications.

items.headline: ACOG releases 2026 maternal immunization schedule, differing from CDC recommendations
items.summary: ACOG issued its first formal maternal vaccine schedule for 2026 that does not align with CDC guidelines. This marks a significant shift in obstetric care recommendations.
items.why_it_matters: Pregnant individuals should discuss vaccination plans with their OB/GYN, as ACOG's new schedule may change which vaccines are recommended during pregnancy.

items.headline: Post-surgery confusion linked to future memory problems in older adults
items.summary: Older adults who experience delirium after surgery are twice as likely to develop long-term cognitive decline. This risk remains even after accounting for other health conditions.
items.why_it_matters: If you or a loved one has surgery, ask your doctor about monitoring for postoperative confusion to address potential cognitive decline early.

items.headline: Removing fallopian tubes during routine surgery may lower ovarian cancer risk
items.summary: The European Society of Gynaecological Oncology recommends removing fallopian tubes during other gynecological surgeries to prevent ovarian cancer. This safe approach is now widely supported.
items.why_it_matters: Women having routine gynecological surgery should discuss removing fallopian tubes with their doctor to reduce ovarian cancer risk.

items.headline: FDA approves new drug for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia patients
items.summary: The FDA approved a new medication to treat agitation in Alzheimer's dementia. This provides a new treatment option for a common and distressing symptom.
items.why_it_matters: Families and caregivers of Alzheimer's patients now have a new treatment option for managing agitation, improving daily care and quality of life.

items.headline: WHO prequalifies first malaria treatment for infants under six months
items.summary: WHO prequalified a new malaria treatment designed for infants under six months. This is the first such treatment approved for this age group.
items.why_it_matters: Parents in malaria areas should seek immediate care for infants with fever, as a new infant-specific treatment is now available through health programs.

items.headline: Memory Changes May Predict Heart Events 8 Years Early
items.summary: Cognitive decline in older adults may precede cardiovascular events by up to 8 years. This could enable earlier detection of heart risks.
items.why_it_matters: Older adults noticing memory changes should discuss them with their doctor as they may signal future heart risks.

items.headline: Virtual neurology visits as effective as in-person for first-time patient evaluations
items.summary: Virtual neurology visits showed no significant difference in outcomes compared to in-person visits for initial patient evaluations. Patient satisfaction rates were comparable between both methods.
items.why_it_matters: Ask your doctor about virtual options for your first neurology appointment to reduce travel time without compromising care quality.

items.headline: Suicide Mortality Among Adolescents and Young Adults After Launch of a Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
items.summary: This study uses data from the National Vital Statistics System to examine quarterly suicide mortality among individuals aged 15 to 34 years.

items.headline: Datopotamab-deruxtecan extends overall survival in metastatic TNBC
items.summary: TROPION-Breast02 randomised 540 patients with previously-treated triple-negative breast cancer. Median OS 18.4 mo vs 14.0 mo with chemo (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92).
items.why_it_matters: First TROP2-ADC to clear an OS benefit in TNBC. Likely registrational; expect filing inside 12 months.

items.headline: Ozempic-class drug improves fatty liver disease in nearly two-thirds of patients
items.summary: In an 800-person trial running 18 months, weekly semaglutide (the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy) cleared fatty-liver inflammation in 63% of people vs 34% on placebo. Liver scarring also improved, and weight came down alongside.
items.why_it_matters: Fatty liver disease affects roughly one in four adults and had almost no medical treatment. Now there's one that also helps with weight.

items.headline: Using an extra antibiotic in wound closure for leg fracture surgerysness
items.summary: The study compared whether applying tobramycin and vancomycin powders topically to a surgical incision during closure of definitive fixation was more effective than applying vancomycin powder alone in reducing deep surgical site infection in periarticular tibial fractures.

items.headline: FDA tightens monitoring for new Alzheimer's drug in people with a high-risk gene
items.summary: Real-world data on lecanemab (a new Alzheimer's-disease drug) showed brain swelling in about 1 in 3 patients who carry two copies of the APOE-ε4 gene, vs about 1 in 20 of those without it. The FDA now requires more frequent MRIs and gene-aware consent.
items.why_it_matters: If you or a family member is considering lecanemab, a simple APOE genetic test now meaningfully changes the risk conversation with your doctor.

items.headline: Low-dose colchicine cuts repeat heart attacks by 31% — now in cardiology guidelines
items.summary: Combining two large trials, a cheap, century-old anti-inflammatory pill (0.5 mg of colchicine daily) reduced repeat heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular death by nearly a third in people who already have heart disease. Major cardiology groups have added it to standard care.
items.why_it_matters: If you've had a heart attack or have known coronary disease, this is a $10/month addition that's now backed by guidelines. Ask your cardiologist whether it fits your medications.

items.headline: Low-dose rapamycin once a week improved immune response in healthy older adults
items.summary: In 120 healthy adults aged 50-85, 5 mg of rapamycin once a week for 11 months raised flu-vaccine antibody response by 22% and reduced markers of immune aging. No serious side effects.
items.why_it_matters: First well-run trial in healthy aging to show an immune benefit. Still early — the question now is whether the same protocol affects real-world infection or hospitalisation rates.

items.headline: KRAS-G12D inhibitor MRTX1133: 41% ORR in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
items.summary: First-in-human Phase 1, n=78, heavily pre-treated PDAC. Objective response 41%, disease control 71%. Median PFS 7.4 months — unprecedented in this setting.
items.why_it_matters: KRAS-G12D drives ~40% of pancreatic cancers. If Phase 3 confirms even half the effect, this is a generational shift in PDAC.

items.headline: One injection a year cut bad cholesterol roughly in half — for the whole year
items.summary: A new gene-silencing therapy delivered as a single shot dropped LDL ('bad') cholesterol by 51% and held that drop steady for 12 months, in a 400-person Phase 2 trial. Two doses across two years matched what monthly cholesterol injections do today.
items.why_it_matters: If approved, this turns cholesterol control from a daily pill or monthly injection into a once-yearly visit — far easier to stick with.

items.headline: Single psilocybin session helps depression that didn't respond to standard drugs
items.summary: In a 300-person Phase 3 trial in treatment-resistant depression, one 25 mg dose of psilocybin (with psychological support) brought 31% of patients into remission at 6 weeks, vs 14% on placebo. The effect held through week 12 with no additional doses.
items.why_it_matters: For people whose depression hasn't responded to two or more standard antidepressants, this is the first Phase 3 win for a psychedelic. FDA decision expected 2027.

items.headline: Metformin extended-release: 4 specific lots recalled for trace impurity
items.summary: Aurobindo Pharma is pulling four lots of extended-release metformin (the most-prescribed diabetes pill) after small amounts of a probable carcinogen were detected. Other lots and other brands are unaffected.
items.why_it_matters: Don't stop the drug. Check your bottle's NDC code against the FDA notice — if it matches, your pharmacy will switch you to a different generic or to immediate-release.

items.headline: Just 150 minutes of brisk walking a week cuts early death by a quarter
items.summary: A pooled study of 1.4 million people found that hitting the standard 150 minutes a week of moderate exercise (think brisk walking, easy cycling) reduced the chance of dying early by 27%. Going beyond about 300 minutes didn't help much more — the big jump happens between zero and the first 150.
items.why_it_matters: If you're sedentary, the first short walks each week are the most valuable thing you can do for your lifespan.
